tone_statements.quote: 4.1.1 Suprasegmental Deverbal Nouns. Certain nouns can be derived from verbs in the language by tonal changes alone. These include: (4) a. sèle ‘to aid’ (V) sélé ‘aid’ (N) b. bòso ‘to rot’ (V) bósó ‘rot’ (N) [...] The data in 4 (a-e) clearly indicates that tone raising of the base verb forms derives nominal forms for this set of data. For this set of data, tone clearly performs morphological functions, as it is the only factor responsible for changing the verbs into nouns.

tone_statements.citation: Ukaegbu, Nkechi M., Gideon S. Omachonu & Benita C. Odii. 2017. An autosegmental analysis of Berom tones and tonal processes. JOLAN: Journal of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria 20(1): 233-242.
tone_statements.quote: Tones play a very significant role in Berom. Tones have the tendency to influence segments, syllables, morphemes and even words in Berom. Berom exploits three (3) distinctive register tones- High [ˊ], mid [ˉ ], low [ ˋ ] and two contour tones: rising [ ˇ ] and falling [ ̂ ] tones; both of which perform lexical and grammatical functions.
tone_statements.locator: Abstract, p. 233 (restated under 'Tones in Berom', p. 237: 'Berom attests three basic register tones- high.. mid.. low.. and two contour tones- falling.. and rising')

sources.citation: Ukaegbu, Nkechi M., Gideon S. Omachonu & Benita C. Odii. 2017. An autosegmental analysis of Berom tones and tonal processes. JOLAN: Journal of the Linguistic Association of Nigeria 20(1): 233-242.
sources.note: Riyom dialect. Three register tones H/M/L plus rising and falling contour tones, lexically and grammatically contrastive; TBUs are vowels and syllabic nasals; tone copying and tonal replacement. 'Stress' appears only in a generic remark that autosegmental theory cannot handle stress; nothing said about Berom stress.

tone.locator: Abstract, p. 233 (restated under 'Tones in Berom', p. 237: 'Berom attests three basic register tones- high.. mid.. low.. and two contour tones- falling.. and rising')
tone.says: Three distinctive register tones (H, M, L) plus rising and falling contour tones, all lexically and grammatically contrastive (minimal triplets given); TBUs are vowels and syllabic nasals; two tonal processes analysed autosegmentally: tone copying (toneless plural prefix be- copies the root tone) and tonal replacement (a H tonal morpheme replaces root tones).

sources.quote: 4.1.1 Suprasegmental Deverbal Nouns. Certain nouns can be derived from verbs in the language by tonal changes alone. These include: (4) a. sèle ‘to aid’ (V) sélé ‘aid’ (N) b. bòso ‘to rot’ (V) bósó ‘rot’ (N) [...] The data in 4 (a-e) clearly indicates that tone raising of the base verb forms derives nominal forms for this set of data. For this set of data, tone clearly performs morphological functions, as it is the only factor responsible for changing the verbs into nouns.
sources.note: Morpho-semantic study of nominalization; section 4.1.1 'Suprasegmental deverbal nouns' documents derivation of nouns from verbs by tone raising alone (sèle 'to aid' > sélé 'aid', bòso 'to rot' > bósó 'rot', tolo > tóló, dak > dák, nara > nára) and concludes tone is a non-segmental derivational marker in Berom; cites Hyman on tonal morphology. No tone inventory or phonology section.

sources.note: Three-volume Birom (Berom, Du dialect, 1960s fieldwork) dictionary by the author of La langue birom 1970. Content not seen (print only). Roulon-Doko's 2006 review states that Birom noun-class marks are 'le plus souvent des infixes ou des variations tonales', so class/number alternants (including tonal ones) are cross-referenced to a main entry, and that entries follow a phonological rather than alphabetical order. That the lexicon is fully tone-marked and what tone inventory the front matter gives are reasonable expectations from Bouquiaux's other work but were not verified.
